# Streaming meeting media — 2026-10-22

This supersedes the raw-spool limitation in `media-finalization-readiness.md`.
Original REC-001/REC-003 still require provider-backed recordings and practical
meeting-duration acceptance. The preceding valid-media checkpoint could hold
only about 1.4 seconds of 1080p RGB frames. Increasing that raw spool limit would
not make it a meeting recorder.

## Data path

`captureToFile` reads one bounded audio/video chunk per pump and writes to two
FFmpeg pipe descriptors concurrently. Each pump awaits the pipe write callback
before requesting another chunk. FFmpeg input queues are limited to four packets;
video uses two threads, zero-latency H.264, and one-second fragmented MP4 output.
Only encoded output reaches disk, under a configured byte quota. WAV header
lengths are patched with bounded header reads. Full independent output inspection
and decoding remain mandatory. No `-fs` truncation can masquerade as success.

The worker uses an owned file artifact, and shared storage uploads consume its
64 KiB stream. Artifact disposal covers successful upload, upload failure,
preflight failure, worker cancellation, and file readers. The existing buffer
capture API remains a bounded compatibility wrapper. The worker's
`cancelCaptures()` cancels active media and disposes retained artifacts; callers
must stop dequeuing jobs before invoking it. Successful recordings still become
ready only after validation and upload/persistence.

Default encoded-file quota is 1 GiB (configurable below 4 GiB), with no default
cumulative raw-byte limit. An optional `maxInputBytes` quota remains supported;
`maxChunkBytes` defaults to 64 MiB. The buffer wrapper defaults to 64 MiB and
cannot exceed 256 MiB. Capture deadline defaults to four hours; after ingress EOF
encoder draining has a 60-second deadline. Probe and full decoder each have a
60-second deadline and respond to capture cancellation. These are resource gates,
not proof that every four-hour meeting or complex high-resolution workload fits.

## Backpressure and failures

Built-in Zoom ingress copies SDK-owned buffers and bounds each stream queue to
32 MiB. Meet/Teams bound queued/in-progress blob bytes and Node-side stream bytes
to 8 MiB each. Overflow fails visibly with a platform capture error; no media is
dropped or silently replaced. Browser arrays have JS representation overhead,
so byte quotas are not equivalent to process RSS. Provider SDK/browser internals
and arbitrary custom producers must also honor their own resource contracts.

The real-time transcription branch uses a coordinated bounded split (8 MiB per
branch plus one pending chunk), rather than native tee's potentially unlimited
slow-consumer backlog. Normalization is pull-driven. Slow downstream consumers
backpressure the source; live push producers that cannot keep up fail at their
explicit queue limit. This does not add ASR codec support.

Failure of either pump, encoder exit, explicit abort, deadline, invalid frame,
or output quota cancels both readers and terminates/awaits the owned process.
The first-frame handshake validates each stream independently, so malformed audio
does not wait indefinitely for a stalled video producer. Temporary output is
removed on failure, and no partial recording is registered.

## Evidence and limits

Reproducible fixture: `media-streaming-acceptance.mjs`, run with
`node --max-old-space-size=128`. It generates media faster than real time, runs
full decoder validation, streams to the shared native local-storage adapter,
compares SHA-256 across upload/download, and independently counts decoded frames.
It reports generated duration separately from actual elapsed time, resolution,
frame count, sampled Node/child RSS, and output bytes. Colors are low-complexity
synthetic RGB frames, not a real meeting or representative camera motion.

The first 128 MiB old-space run exposed retained cancellation-promise handlers
per read/write. Replacing repeated `Promise.race` calls against one unresolved
promise with reader cancellation/process termination removed that growth; the
same one-hour fixture then passed without increasing the heap allowance.

Remaining requirements include real Zoom frame-layout conversion/acceptance,
Meet/Teams video, desktop container correctness, per-participant recording,
encoded-ASR support, PCM discontinuity/timeline policy, complex-motion and
provider-paced acceptance, production disk provisioning/recovery after process
crash, and operational deployments. Nothing here proves live provider recording.

## Measured receipts

Final local receipt: `media-streaming-receipt-20261022.json`. Commands used
128 MiB V8 old-space, whose reported total V8 heap limit was 184,549,376 bytes.
RSS includes external buffers and is reported separately. Values are sampled,
not guaranteed absolute process peaks.

| Fixture | Generated media | Raw ingress | Capture + full validation | After both producer EOF | Total incl. storage/hash/frame count | Node RSS / child RSS | Encoded bytes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Long duration | 3600 s, 64×64, 30 fps, 108000 frames | 1,442,304,000 B | 42.666 s | 4.074 s | 43.735 s | 108,183,552 / 37,289,984 B | 30,749,416 |
| Full resolution | 30 s, 1920×1080, 30 fps, 900 frames | 5,599,680,000 B | 3.098 s | 0.218 s | 3.902 s | 143,015,936 / 157,270,016 B | 608,985 |

Both have 16 kHz mono PCM input, AAC output, exact expected independently decoded
video frame counts, and matching stored/downloaded SHA-256. AAC priming extends
container durations to 3600.064063 and 30.064063 seconds. The post-EOF interval
includes queued ingress drain and full validation; total time additionally
includes local storage upload/download hash comparison and independent frame
count. Other parallel tasks were present on the host. These are acceptance
measurements, not a representative production benchmark or cloud-storage SLA.

Zero-latency encoding reduced the earlier sampled 1080p child working set from
458 MB to about 157 MB. Neither fixture extrapolates to one-hour complex 1080p
camera motion. Per-session disk quotas also require deployment-wide admission
and disk-capacity policy; they do not impose a global multi-session quota.


Storage streaming removes full-file buffering, but signed-URL upload still needs
an explicit operation deadline and response-body lifecycle policy. A stalled
remote upload can retain its artifact beyond capture deadlines. This remains a
storage-operation bound to implement; capture limits do not imply upload limits.

## Validation receipt

Server: 239 tests across 43 files; core 51, Zoom 25, Meet 11, Teams 9,
TypeScript client 12, Python client 14. Core/platform/server/client TypeScript
builds pass. Tests cover buffer and file APIs, actual signed HTTP upload,
artifact cleanup on preflight/storage failure, zero/nonzero encoder exit while
both inputs stall, abort/limits, active file-reader disposal, SDK/browser overflow,
bounded audio split and unconsumed-ASR cleanup. No dependency/lockfile changes.
Logs: `/tmp/rec-stream-full-tests.log`, `/tmp/rec-stream-all-adapter-tests.log`,
`/tmp/rec-stream-python-tests.log`, `/tmp/rec-stream-builds.log`, and
`/tmp/rec-stream-final-build.log`.
# Bounded recording uploads — 2026-10-22

`uploadObject`, `uploadRecording`, and `createBotWorker` now accept
`uploadTimeoutMs`. The default is 300000 ms (five minutes); values must be positive
integer milliseconds no larger than 2147483647. The deadline covers adapter
acquisition or URL signing, input reads, backpressured writes, close, HTTP request,
and response-body cancellation. `UploadOptions` and `UploadRecordingInput` also
accept an `AbortSignal`; worker shutdown propagates its session cancellation into
an in-progress upload. Existing manual-upload routes use the finite default.

The streaming path owns a reader and writer, awaits each write before reading
another chunk, and removes per-operation cancellation listeners. Timeout or caller
cancellation cancels its reader, releases stream locks, requests writable abort,
and returns without waiting indefinitely for the adapter. Late stream acquisition
is observed and aborted without writing. Native fetch receives the abort signal;
HTTP response bodies are cancelled after their status is received, including
unbounded successful bodies. Upload consumes and disposes the native capture
artifact on success and failure.

## External effects and limits

The shared `StorageAdapter` acquisition/signing methods do not accept a signal.
A custom adapter can continue after timeout. Web Streams defer underlying sink
abort until a pending write settles; an adapter whose write never settles can
retain its own resources despite the caller returning. This change does not claim
that such an operation was stopped or rolled back. Late promises have rejection
handlers, and bounded caller lifetime does not establish remote object absence.

The pre-existing producer intent remains `uncertain` after timeout/cancellation.
No recording row or ready event is produced. A late sink completion does not clear
that intent. Operators must establish that the original external operation stopped
before invoking the existing reconciliation workflow. Timeout alone is not proof.

These bounds cover the storage operation, not database operations, platform leave,
metadata retrieval, or arbitrary user-provided artifact disposal. The owned native
capture artifact destroys and awaits its local file readers before removal. Hosts
still need broader lifecycle and database bounds. There are no shared adapter
interface changes, new dependencies, remote storage acceptance, or live meetings.

## Reproduction and evidence

Run from the repository root:

```
npm test --workspace=@recfn/server -- --run
npm run build --workspace=@recfn/server
```

`upload-deadline.test.ts` uses real timers, native localhost HTTP servers and an
FFmpeg-created WAV file artifact. The stalled sink fixture leaves `write()` pending
through a 100 ms deadline. The caller returns, the artifact directory is empty,
locks are released, no recording exists, and the producer remains uncertain.
The sink's abort has not run at that point. Releasing the owned test write then
allows abort to run; uncertainty remains unchanged.

The native HTTP receiver accepts 1024 bytes and withholds the response. The 300 ms
deadline rejects and the receiver observes connection closure. A second receiver
sends 200 headers and an unending body; cancellation closes that connection while
the successful upload returns. Fixtures close their owned listeners/connections.
Other cases cover late stream acquisition, shutdown during a pending read, and
invalid deadline values.

The worker lifecycle tests exercise both the configured deadline and explicit
`cancelCaptures()` while a sink write is pending. Both finish in error, retain the
uncertain intent, emit no finalization-complete result, and remove local artifacts.

Validation: 251 server tests across 44 files passed; server typecheck and build
passed. Logs: `/tmp/rec-upload-server-tests.log`, `/tmp/rec-upload-build.log`.
Only TypeScript server upload/lifecycle code changes; Python and TypeScript client
wire APIs and platform/media contracts are unchanged.
# RecFn persistence boundary — 2026-10-19

This slice implements the shared database boundary from the original phase 00 and TV-ARCH-001 requirements. It does not establish overall production readiness.

## Behavior

- `createDbStore` owns `wrapWithSchema(adapter, getRecFnSchema())`. Applications supply a normal shared adapter; `adapterSchema` is not required.
- Durability defaults false. A caller must explicitly assert that its configured backend persists across restarts. The built-in memory adapter rejects `durable: true`, including when its display name is overridden. The existing production guard remains in place.
- Schema metadata declares JSON text and ISO date text, preserving structured runtime values and canonical ISO timestamps. Meeting metadata has a unique namespace/bot index. Participant, metadata, and calendar mapping upserts use explicit conflict targets.
- Shared dependency versions now resolve to the local shared stack rather than stale nested DB/HTTP/storage/middleware packages. The root lock changes only the RecFn server dependency closure.

## Native SQLite evidence

`server/__tests__/db-sqlite.test.ts` creates an actual file-backed better-sqlite3 database, applies tables/indexes from the exported schema, and uses the shared Kysely adapter without caller schema configuration. It writes bots, recordings, transcripts, participants, chat, metadata, webhooks, calendars, and event/bot mappings; closes the adapter; opens a new database connection and store; and verifies aggregate content, nested JSON, Unicode, canonical dates, boolean values, upsert updates, and namespace isolation. It deletes a bot aggregate, closes/reopens again, verifies deletion and retention of another namespace, and checks that an actual missing-table error propagates. Temporary databases are removed in finally.

The existing memory test now explicitly describes reuse across store instances; it is not durability evidence. SQLite close/reopen proves persistence across connections, but this test does not restart a server process, exercise crash recovery, validate a hosted database, or certify production backups.

## Validation

- Node 20.20.0, npm 10.8.2; lock regenerated with npm 11 and scoped clean installation completed with npm 10. Native better-sqlite3 and esbuild rebuild passed.
- Shared DB build and complete suite: **220 tests passed in 22 files**. Prerequisite commits: `517a4f8d0` (Kysely conflict targets/returning) and `1073a1329` (declared SQLite boolean codecs).
- `npm test -w @recfn/server -- __tests__/db-store.test.ts __tests__/db-sqlite.test.ts __tests__/api-recordings.test.ts __tests__/storage-adapter.test.ts`: **20 tests passed in 4 files**.
- Scoped strict TypeScript check for `server/src/store/db.ts` and `server/src/store/schema.ts`: passed (`--noEmit --target ES2022 --module ESNext --moduleResolution bundler --strict --skipLibCheck --esModuleInterop`).
- Complete dependency builds reach the server, which fails at unchanged `server/src/webhooks/deliver.ts:37`: the consumer passes `fetch`, but shared `WebhookDeliveryOptions` intentionally has no custom-fetch option. Both source files match base `9b841ff4a`. No shared transport behavior was changed here.

not make it a meeting recorder.

## Data path

`captureToFile` reads one bounded audio/video chunk per pump and writes to two
FFmpeg pipe descriptors concurrently. Each pump awaits the pipe write callback
before requesting another chunk. FFmpeg input queues are limited to four packets;
video uses two threads, zero-latency H.264, and one-second fragmented MP4 output.
Only encoded output reaches disk, under a configured byte quota. WAV header
lengths are patched with bounded header reads. Full independent output inspection
and decoding remain mandatory. No `-fs` truncation can masquerade as success.

The worker uses an owned file artifact, and shared storage uploads consume its
64 KiB stream. Artifact disposal covers successful upload, upload failure,
preflight failure, worker cancellation, and file readers. The existing buffer
capture API remains a bounded compatibility wrapper. The worker's
`cancelCaptures()` cancels active media and disposes retained artifacts; callers
must stop dequeuing jobs before invoking it. Successful recordings still become
ready only after validation and upload/persistence.

Default encoded-file quota is 1 GiB (configurable below 4 GiB), with no default
cumulative raw-byte limit. An optional `maxInputBytes` quota remains supported;
`maxChunkBytes` defaults to 64 MiB. The buffer wrapper defaults to 64 MiB and
cannot exceed 256 MiB. Capture deadline defaults to four hours; after ingress EOF
encoder draining has a 60-second deadline. Probe and full decoder each have a
60-second deadline and respond to capture cancellation. These are resource gates,
not proof that every four-hour meeting or complex high-resolution workload fits.

## Backpressure and failures

Built-in Zoom ingress copies SDK-owned buffers and bounds each stream queue to
32 MiB. Meet/Teams bound queued/in-progress blob bytes and Node-side stream bytes
to 8 MiB each. Overflow fails visibly with a platform capture error; no media is
dropped or silently replaced. Browser arrays have JS representation overhead,
so byte quotas are not equivalent to process RSS. Provider SDK/browser internals
and arbitrary custom producers must also honor their own resource contracts.

The real-time transcription branch uses a coordinated bounded split (8 MiB per
branch plus one pending chunk), rather than native tee's potentially unlimited
slow-consumer backlog. Normalization is pull-driven. Slow downstream consumers
backpressure the source; live push producers that cannot keep up fail at their
explicit queue limit. This does not add ASR codec support.

Failure of either pump, encoder exit, explicit abort, deadline, invalid frame,
or output quota cancels both readers and terminates/awaits the owned process.
The first-frame handshake validates each stream independently, so malformed audio
does not wait indefinitely for a stalled video producer. Temporary output is
removed on failure, and no partial recording is registered.

## Evidence and limits

Reproducible fixture: `media-streaming-acceptance.mjs`, run with
`node --max-old-space-size=128`. It generates media faster than real time, runs
full decoder validation, streams to the shared native local-storage adapter,
compares SHA-256 across upload/download, and independently counts decoded frames.
It reports generated duration separately from actual elapsed time, resolution,
frame count, sampled Node/child RSS, and output bytes. Colors are low-complexity
synthetic RGB frames, not a real meeting or representative camera motion.

The first 128 MiB old-space run exposed retained cancellation-promise handlers
per read/write. Replacing repeated `Promise.race` calls against one unresolved
promise with reader cancellation/process termination removed that growth; the
same one-hour fixture then passed without increasing the heap allowance.

Remaining requirements include real Zoom frame-layout conversion/acceptance,
Meet/Teams video, desktop container correctness, per-participant recording,
encoded-ASR support, PCM discontinuity/timeline policy, complex-motion and
provider-paced acceptance, production disk provisioning/recovery after process
crash, and operational deployments. Nothing here proves live provider recording.

Final local receipt: `media-streaming-receipt-20261022.json`. Commands used
128 MiB V8 old-space, whose reported total V8 heap limit was 184,549,376 bytes.
RSS includes external buffers and is reported separately. Values are sampled,
not guaranteed absolute process peaks.

video frame counts, and matching stored/downloaded SHA-256. AAC priming extends
container durations to 3600.064063 and 30.064063 seconds. The post-EOF interval
includes queued ingress drain and full validation; total time additionally
includes local storage upload/download hash comparison and independent frame
count. Other parallel tasks were present on the host. These are acceptance
measurements, not a representative production benchmark or cloud-storage SLA.

Zero-latency encoding reduced the earlier sampled 1080p child working set from
458 MB to about 157 MB. Neither fixture extrapolates to one-hour complex 1080p
camera motion. Per-session disk quotas also require deployment-wide admission
and disk-capacity policy; they do not impose a global multi-session quota.


Storage streaming removes full-file buffering, but signed-URL upload still needs
an explicit operation deadline and response-body lifecycle policy. A stalled
remote upload can retain its artifact beyond capture deadlines. This remains a
storage-operation bound to implement; capture limits do not imply upload limits.

`/tmp/rec-stream-python-tests.log`, `/tmp/rec-stream-builds.log`, and
`/tmp/rec-stream-final-build.log`.
# Bounded recording uploads — 2026-10-22

`uploadObject`, `uploadRecording`, and `createBotWorker` now accept
`uploadTimeoutMs`. The default is 300000 ms (five minutes); values must be positive
integer milliseconds no larger than 2147483647. The deadline covers adapter
acquisition or URL signing, input reads, backpressured writes, close, HTTP request,
and response-body cancellation. `UploadOptions` and `UploadRecordingInput` also
accept an `AbortSignal`; worker shutdown propagates its session cancellation into
an in-progress upload. Existing manual-upload routes use the finite default.

The streaming path owns a reader and writer, awaits each write before reading
another chunk, and removes per-operation cancellation listeners. Timeout or caller
cancellation cancels its reader, releases stream locks, requests writable abort,
and returns without waiting indefinitely for the adapter. Late stream acquisition
is observed and aborted without writing. Native fetch receives the abort signal;
HTTP response bodies are cancelled after their status is received, including
unbounded successful bodies. Upload consumes and disposes the native capture
artifact on success and failure.

The shared `StorageAdapter` acquisition/signing methods do not accept a signal.
A custom adapter can continue after timeout. Web Streams defer underlying sink
abort until a pending write settles; an adapter whose write never settles can
retain its own resources despite the caller returning. This change does not claim
that such an operation was stopped or rolled back. Late promises have rejection
handlers, and bounded caller lifetime does not establish remote object absence.

The pre-existing producer intent remains `uncertain` after timeout/cancellation.
No recording row or ready event is produced. A late sink completion does not clear
that intent. Operators must establish that the original external operation stopped
before invoking the existing reconciliation workflow. Timeout alone is not proof.

These bounds cover the storage operation, not database operations, platform leave,
metadata retrieval, or arbitrary user-provided artifact disposal. The owned native
capture artifact destroys and awaits its local file readers before removal. Hosts
still need broader lifecycle and database bounds. There are no shared adapter
interface changes, new dependencies, remote storage acceptance, or live meetings.

The native HTTP receiver accepts 1024 bytes and withholds the response. The 300 ms

The worker lifecycle tests exercise both the configured deadline and explicit

Superfunctions is a **Turbo monorepo** containing self-hosted developer tools and libraries. The repository is organized into:

## Recording capture and storage

### REC-001
- **Priority**: P0
- **Statement**: The system MUST capture meeting audio/video and produce a recording file in the configured format (MP4 or audio-only).
- **Rationale**: Core recording capability.
- **Acceptance criteria**:
  - After bot leaves, a Recording entity is created with valid format, duration, and size.
  - Recording file is stored in filefn/storage.
  - downloadUrl is a signed, time-limited URL.
- **Test vectors**: TV-REC-001
- **Notes**: MP4 is default. Audio-only produces WAV or OPUS.

### REC-002
- **Priority**: P1
- **Statement**: The system SHOULD capture separate audio tracks per participant where the platform allows.
- **Rationale**: Recall.ai feature parity; enables better diarization and per-participant analytics.
- **Acceptance criteria**:
  - For platforms supporting per-participant audio (Zoom), separate audio files are stored.
  - For platforms that don't support it, a single mixed audio track is stored.
  - Per-participant tracks are accessible via the recordings API.
- **Test vectors**: TV-REC-002
- **Notes**: Platform-dependent. Zoom supports separate tracks natively.

### REC-003
- **Priority**: P0
- **Statement**: Recordings MUST be uploaded to filefn/storage within 60 seconds of the bot leaving the meeting.
- **Rationale**: Performance constraint from requirements.
- **Acceptance criteria**:
  - Time from bot `left` to recording available (storageRef populated) is <60s for recordings up to 1 hour.
  - Longer recordings MAY take proportionally longer.
- **Test vectors**: TV-REC-003
- **Notes**: Upload is queued via flowfn for reliability.

### REC-004
- **Priority**: P0
- **Statement**: Recordings MUST be encrypted at rest via the storage adapter.
- **Rationale**: Security hard constraint.
- **Acceptance criteria**:
  - Storage adapter is configured with encryption (e.g., S3 server-side encryption).
  - Raw recording bytes are not stored in plaintext on disk (unless local dev mode with explicit opt-out).
- **Test vectors**: TV-SEC-003
- **Notes**: Encryption delegated to filefn/storage adapter.

### REC-005
- **Priority**: P0

## Recording capture and storage

### REC-001
- **Priority**: P0
- **Statement**: The system MUST capture meeting audio/video and produce a recording file in the configured format (MP4 or audio-only).
- **Rationale**: Core recording capability.
- **Acceptance criteria**:
  - After bot leaves, a Recording entity is created with valid format, duration, and size.
  - Recording file is stored in filefn/storage.
  - downloadUrl is a signed, time-limited URL.
- **Test vectors**: TV-REC-001
- **Notes**: MP4 is default. Audio-only produces WAV or OPUS.

### REC-002
- **Priority**: P1
- **Statement**: The system SHOULD capture separate audio tracks per participant where the platform allows.
- **Rationale**: Recall.ai feature parity; enables better diarization and per-participant analytics.
- **Acceptance criteria**:
  - For platforms supporting per-participant audio (Zoom), separate audio files are stored.
  - For platforms that don't support it, a single mixed audio track is stored.
  - Per-participant tracks are accessible via the recordings API.
- **Test vectors**: TV-REC-002
- **Notes**: Platform-dependent. Zoom supports separate tracks natively.

### REC-003
- **Priority**: P0
- **Statement**: Recordings MUST be uploaded to filefn/storage within 60 seconds of the bot leaving the meeting.
- **Rationale**: Performance constraint from requirements.
- **Acceptance criteria**:
  - Time from bot `left` to recording available (storageRef populated) is <60s for recordings up to 1 hour.
  - Longer recordings MAY take proportionally longer.
- **Test vectors**: TV-REC-003
- **Notes**: Upload is queued via flowfn for reliability.

### REC-004
- **Priority**: P0
- **Statement**: Recordings MUST be encrypted at rest via the storage adapter.
- **Rationale**: Security hard constraint.
- **Acceptance criteria**:
  - Storage adapter is configured with encryption (e.g., S3 server-side encryption).
  - Raw recording bytes are not stored in plaintext on disk (unless local dev mode with explicit opt-out).
- **Test vectors**: TV-SEC-003
- **Notes**: Encryption delegated to filefn/storage adapter.

### REC-005
- **Priority**: P0

# AGENTS.md - AI Agent Development Guide for Superfunctions

> **Purpose**: This document provides AI agents with essential information for working effectively on the Superfunctions monorepo.

## 🏗️ Repository Structure

Superfunctions is a **Turbo monorepo** containing self-hosted developer tools and libraries. The repository is organized into:

### Core Functions (Top-Level Directories)

Individual superfunction packages, each providing specific developer capabilities:

- **`authfn/`** - Authentication & API key management
- **`cachefn/`** - Multi-tier caching with function memoization
- **`drawfn/`** - Cross-framework drawing canvas for brainstorming
- **`plugfn/`** - Integration platform (OAuth, webhooks, 75+ providers)
- **`searchfn/`** - Browser-first full-text search with IndexedDB
- **`secfn/`** - Security functions (secrets vault, rate limiting, monitoring)
- **`testfn/`** - Testing utilities and frameworks
- **`botfn/`** - Bot framework (Discord, GitHub, Linear integrations)
- **`hostfn/`** - Hosting and deployment utilities
- **`uifn/`** - UI components and utilities
- **`watchfn/`** - File watching and monitoring
- **`billfn/`** - Billing and payment processing
- **`browsefn/`** - Browser automation utilities
- **`chartfn/`** - Charting and visualization
- **`datafn/`** - Data processing utilities
- **`docsfn/`** - Documentation generation
- **`filefn/`** - File operations and management
- **`flowfn/`** - Flow control (queues, streams, workflows)
- **`iconfn/`** - Icon utilities
- **`logfn/`** - Logging utilities
- **`mailfn/`** - Programmable real inboxes for products, agents, and tests
- **`sendfn/`** - Email/messaging utilities

### Shared Packages (`packages/`)

Framework-agnostic core libraries used across superfunctions:

**TypeScript Packages:**

- `@superfunctions/http` - HTTP abstractions
- `@superfunctions/http-express` - Express.js adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-fastify` - Fastify adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-hono` - Hono adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-next` - Next.js adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-sveltekit` - SvelteKit adapter
- `@superfunctions/db` - Database adapter system (Drizzle, Prisma, Kysely)
- `@superfunctions/auth` - Authentication abstraction layer
- `@superfunctions/cli` - CLI tool for schema management

**Python Packages:**

- `superfunctions` (from `python-core/`) - Core namespace package
- `superfunctions-sqlalchemy` (from `python-sqlalchemy/`)
- `superfunctions-fastapi` (from `python-fastapi/`)
- `superfunctions-flask` (from `python-flask/`)

### Other Directories

- **`_conduct/`** - Root-level artifacts for shared code (implementation plans, specs, audits)
- **`21n/`** - Organization-specific packages
- **`.agent/`** - Agent workflows and automation
- **`.github/`** - GitHub Actions and CI/CD

## 📦 Package Naming Conventions

### Rule A: Shared Packages Format

**Any package shared across superfunctions uses `@superfunctions/{name}` format**

Examples:

```
packages/db/          → @superfunctions/db
packages/http/        → @superfunctions/http
packages/auth/        → @superfunctions/auth
packages/cli/         → @superfunctions/cli
```

### Rule B: Core Function Packages Format

**Single-package functions**: Use simple name without scope

```
authfn/ts-sdk/        → authfn
drawfn/core/          → drawfn
cachefn/typescript/   → cachefn
plugfn/core/         → plugfn
searchfn/             → searchfn
```

**Multi-package functions**: Use `@{functionname}/{sub-package}` format (if needed in future)

```
@authfn/core          (example for future multi-package structure)
@authfn/providers     (example for future multi-package structure)
```

**Current Status**: All core functions currently use single-package structure. The scoped format is reserved for future expansion if a function needs multiple published packages.

### Rule C: Monorepo Structure

**The root `superfunctions` is a Turbo monorepo. Avoid nested monorepos.**

- ✅ Use subfolders to organize functions (e.g., `authfn/python/`, `authfn/ts-sdk/`)
- ❌ Do NOT create nested monorepos (e.g., `authfn/` should NOT be another monorepo)
- ✅ Use Turbo workspaces defined in root `package.json`

Current workspaces:

```json
{
  "workspaces": [
    "searchfn",
    "botfn/*",
    "hostfn/*",
    "authfn/*",
    "packages/*",
    "21n/*"
  ]
}
```

### Rule D: Artifact Location

**Create artifacts (`.md` files) in `.conduct` folders**

- **Function-specific artifacts**: `{function}/.conduct/`
  - Examples: `authfn/.conduct/implementation.md`, `drawfn/.conduct/audit_report.md`
- **Shared/root artifacts**: `_conduct/`
  - Examples: `_conduct/implementation.md`, `_conduct/spec.md`

Artifact types:

- `implementation.md` - Implementation plans
- `spec.md` - Technical specifications
- `audit_report.md` - Code audits and reviews
- `task.md` - Task tracking
- `walkthrough.md` - Feature walkthroughs

## 🗂️ Language Support

Most core functions support **both TypeScript and Python**:

### TypeScript Structure

```
{function}/
├── typescript/       or  core/
│   ├── src/
│   ├── package.json
│   ├── tsconfig.json
│   └── vitest.config.ts
```

### Python Structure

```
{function}/
├── python/
│   ├── {function}/        # Python package directory
│   │   ├── __init__.py
│   │   └── ...
│   ├── tests/
│   ├── pyproject.toml
│   └── README.md
```

### Examples

- `authfn/typescript/` + `authfn/python/`
- `cachefn/typescript/` + `cachefn/python/`
- `secfn/typescript/` + `secfn/python/`
- `plugfn/core/` + `plugfn/python/`
- `drawfn/core/` (TypeScript only, with React/Svelte adapters)
- `searchfn/` (TypeScript only, browser-focused)

```bash
# Build all packages
npm run build

# Build specific package (from root)
turbo run build --filter=authfn
turbo run build --filter=@superfunctions/db

# Build from package directory
cd authfn/ts-sdk && npm run build
```

### Testing

```bash
# Test all packages
npm test

# Test specific package
turbo run test --filter=drawfn

# Watch mode
npm run test:watch
```

### Linting

```bash
npm run lint
```

### Package Manager

- **npm** (v10.2.0+) - Specified in `packageManager` field
- Uses npm workspaces for monorepo management
- Turbo for build orchestration

## 🎯 Key Superfunctions Features

### AuthFn

- Multi-provider authentication (OAuth, API keys, JWT)
- Framework-agnostic with adapters for Express, Fastify, Hono, Next.js, SvelteKit
- Database-agnostic (Drizzle, Prisma, Kysely)

- Access control and permissions
- Rate limiting

- Secret scanning

### BotFn

- Multi-platform bot framework
- Discord, GitHub, Linear integrations

- Event-driven architecture

## 🛠️ Common Tasks

### Adding a New Function

1. Create top-level directory: `{functionname}/`
2. Add TypeScript SDK: `{functionname}/typescript/` or `{functionname}/ts-sdk/`
3. (Optional) Add Python SDK: `{functionname}/python/`
4. Create `.conduct/` for artifacts
5. Add to workspace in root `package.json`
6. Package name: `{functionname}` (not scoped unless multi-package)

### Adding a Shared Package

1. Create in `packages/{name}/`
2. Package name: `@superfunctions/{name}`
3. Add to workspace (already covered by `packages/*`)
4. Update dependent packages

### Creating Artifacts

1. Function-specific: `{function}/.conduct/{artifact}.md`
2. Shared/root: `_conduct/{artifact}.md`
3. Use consistent naming: `implementation.md`, `spec.md`, `audit_report.md`, etc.

### Working with Turbo

```bash
# Run task across all packages
turbo run build
turbo run test

turbo run build --filter=authfn

turbo run build --filter=authfn...
```

## 🚀 Best Practices

### Super functions ecosystem (Very important)

- Reuse shared packages from `packages/` folder like http abstraction, db abstraction, etc.
- Never duplicate shared code like http adapters, db abstractions, etc.
- Don't reexport http-adapters etc - end consumers of the core function package will use the adapters directly. Refer `authfn` implementation for usage of core http router, core db, http adapters and db interface usage.
- Function packages that accept a `@superfunctions/db` `Adapter` must wrap the incoming adapter internally with their own schema, for example `wrapWithSchema(config.database, getSchema(...))`, before passing it to services/storage. Do not require app consumers to pass `adapterSchema` to `drizzleAdapter`, `kyselyAdapter`, `prismaAdapter`, or `memoryAdapter`; `adapterSchema` is a deprecated compatibility escape hatch for direct app-level adapter use.

### Code Organization

- Keep shared code in `packages/`
- Keep function-specific code in `{function}/`
- Use TypeScript for type safety

- Update README.md with usage examples

### Testing

- Use Vitest for TypeScript
- Use pytest for Python
- Maintain high test coverage
- Test adapters separately

- Coordinate versions across language SDKs
- Document migration guides for breaking changes

# AGENTS.md - AI Agent Development Guide for Superfunctions

> **Purpose**: This document provides AI agents with essential information for working effectively on the Superfunctions monorepo.

## 🏗️ Repository Structure

Superfunctions is a **Turbo monorepo** containing self-hosted developer tools and libraries. The repository is organized into:

### Core Functions (Top-Level Directories)

Individual superfunction packages, each providing specific developer capabilities:

- **`authfn/`** - Authentication & API key management
- **`cachefn/`** - Multi-tier caching with function memoization
- **`drawfn/`** - Cross-framework drawing canvas for brainstorming
- **`plugfn/`** - Integration platform (OAuth, webhooks, 75+ providers)
- **`searchfn/`** - Browser-first full-text search with IndexedDB
- **`secfn/`** - Security functions (secrets vault, rate limiting, monitoring)
- **`testfn/`** - Testing utilities and frameworks
- **`botfn/`** - Bot framework (Discord, GitHub, Linear integrations)
- **`hostfn/`** - Hosting and deployment utilities
- **`uifn/`** - UI components and utilities
- **`watchfn/`** - File watching and monitoring
- **`billfn/`** - Billing and payment processing
- **`browsefn/`** - Browser automation utilities
- **`chartfn/`** - Charting and visualization
- **`datafn/`** - Data processing utilities
- **`docsfn/`** - Documentation generation
- **`filefn/`** - File operations and management
- **`flowfn/`** - Flow control (queues, streams, workflows)
- **`iconfn/`** - Icon utilities
- **`logfn/`** - Logging utilities
- **`mailfn/`** - Programmable real inboxes for products, agents, and tests
- **`sendfn/`** - Email/messaging utilities

### Shared Packages (`packages/`)

Framework-agnostic core libraries used across superfunctions:

**TypeScript Packages:**

- `@superfunctions/http` - HTTP abstractions
- `@superfunctions/http-express` - Express.js adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-fastify` - Fastify adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-hono` - Hono adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-next` - Next.js adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-sveltekit` - SvelteKit adapter
- `@superfunctions/db` - Database adapter system (Drizzle, Prisma, Kysely)
- `@superfunctions/auth` - Authentication abstraction layer
- `@superfunctions/cli` - CLI tool for schema management

**Python Packages:**

- `superfunctions` (from `python-core/`) - Core namespace package
- `superfunctions-sqlalchemy` (from `python-sqlalchemy/`)
- `superfunctions-fastapi` (from `python-fastapi/`)
- `superfunctions-flask` (from `python-flask/`)

### Other Directories

- **`_conduct/`** - Root-level artifacts for shared code (implementation plans, specs, audits)
- **`21n/`** - Organization-specific packages
- **`.agent/`** - Agent workflows and automation
- **`.github/`** - GitHub Actions and CI/CD

## 📦 Package Naming Conventions

### Rule A: Shared Packages Format

**Any package shared across superfunctions uses `@superfunctions/{name}` format**

Examples:

```
packages/db/          → @superfunctions/db
packages/http/        → @superfunctions/http
packages/auth/        → @superfunctions/auth
packages/cli/         → @superfunctions/cli
```

### Rule B: Core Function Packages Format

**Single-package functions**: Use simple name without scope

```
authfn/ts-sdk/        → authfn
drawfn/core/          → drawfn
cachefn/typescript/   → cachefn
plugfn/core/         → plugfn
searchfn/             → searchfn
```

**Multi-package functions**: Use `@{functionname}/{sub-package}` format (if needed in future)

```
@authfn/core          (example for future multi-package structure)
@authfn/providers     (example for future multi-package structure)
```

**Current Status**: All core functions currently use single-package structure. The scoped format is reserved for future expansion if a function needs multiple published packages.

### Rule C: Monorepo Structure

**The root `superfunctions` is a Turbo monorepo. Avoid nested monorepos.**

- ✅ Use subfolders to organize functions (e.g., `authfn/python/`, `authfn/ts-sdk/`)
- ❌ Do NOT create nested monorepos (e.g., `authfn/` should NOT be another monorepo)
- ✅ Use Turbo workspaces defined in root `package.json`

Current workspaces:

```json
{
  "workspaces": [
    "searchfn",
    "botfn/*",
    "hostfn/*",
    "authfn/*",
    "packages/*",
    "21n/*"
  ]
}
```

### Rule D: Artifact Location

**Create artifacts (`.md` files) in `.conduct` folders**

- **Function-specific artifacts**: `{function}/.conduct/`
  - Examples: `authfn/.conduct/implementation.md`, `drawfn/.conduct/audit_report.md`
- **Shared/root artifacts**: `_conduct/`
  - Examples: `_conduct/implementation.md`, `_conduct/spec.md`

Artifact types:

- `implementation.md` - Implementation plans
- `spec.md` - Technical specifications
- `audit_report.md` - Code audits and reviews
- `task.md` - Task tracking
- `walkthrough.md` - Feature walkthroughs

## 🗂️ Language Support

Most core functions support **both TypeScript and Python**:

### TypeScript Structure

```
{function}/
├── typescript/       or  core/
│   ├── src/
│   ├── package.json
│   ├── tsconfig.json
│   └── vitest.config.ts
```

### Python Structure

```
{function}/
├── python/
│   ├── {function}/        # Python package directory
│   │   ├── __init__.py
│   │   └── ...
│   ├── tests/
│   ├── pyproject.toml
│   └── README.md
```

### Examples

- `authfn/typescript/` + `authfn/python/`
- `cachefn/typescript/` + `cachefn/python/`
- `secfn/typescript/` + `secfn/python/`
- `plugfn/core/` + `plugfn/python/`
- `drawfn/core/` (TypeScript only, with React/Svelte adapters)
- `searchfn/` (TypeScript only, browser-focused)

## 🔧 Development Workflow

### Building

```bash
# Build all packages
npm run build

# Build specific package (from root)
turbo run build --filter=authfn
turbo run build --filter=@superfunctions/db

# Build from package directory
cd authfn/ts-sdk && npm run build
```

### Testing

```bash
# Test all packages
npm test

# Test specific package
turbo run test --filter=drawfn

# Watch mode
npm run test:watch
```

### Linting

```bash
npm run lint
```

### Package Manager

- **npm** (v10.2.0+) - Specified in `packageManager` field
- Uses npm workspaces for monorepo management
- Turbo for build orchestration

## 🎯 Key Superfunctions Features

### AuthFn

- Multi-provider authentication (OAuth, API keys, JWT)
- Framework-agnostic with adapters for Express, Fastify, Hono, Next.js, SvelteKit
- Database-agnostic (Drizzle, Prisma, Kysely)
- TypeScript + Python SDKs

### DrawFn

- Cross-framework drawing canvas
- React and Svelte adapters
- Scene management, export capabilities
- Tolerant parsing with version validation

### PlugFn

- Self-hosted integration platform
- 75+ provider integrations (GitHub, Slack, Discord, Linear, Stripe)
- OAuth 2.0 flow handling
- Webhook support
- Multi-tenant with secure token storage

### SearchFn

- Browser-first full-text search
- IndexedDB persistence with in-memory LRU cache
- BM25 scoring
- FlexSearch-compatible API
- Worker-ready with snapshot export/import

### MailFn

- Stable and expiring programmable inboxes
- Cloudflare Email Workers, D1, R2, and Queues deployment adapter
- Raw MIME and attachment evidence, waits, OTP/link extraction, threads, labels, and search
- Typed client, test helpers, CLI, MCP server, custom domains, webhooks, and SendFn composition
- Scoped credentials, retention, audit, quotas, and explicitly gated public-platform controls

### CacheFn

- Multi-tier caching (memory, IndexedDB, external)
- Function memoization
- TTL and invalidation strategies
- Browser and server support

### SecFn

- Secrets vault management
- Access control and permissions
- Rate limiting
- Security monitoring
- Secret scanning

### BotFn

- Multi-platform bot framework
- Discord, GitHub, Linear integrations
- Shared types and persistence layer
- Event-driven architecture

## 🛠️ Common Tasks

### Adding a New Function

1. Create top-level directory: `{functionname}/`
2. Add TypeScript SDK: `{functionname}/typescript/` or `{functionname}/ts-sdk/`
3. (Optional) Add Python SDK: `{functionname}/python/`
4. Create `.conduct/` for artifacts
5. Add to workspace in root `package.json`
6. Package name: `{functionname}` (not scoped unless multi-package)

### Adding a Shared Package

1. Create in `packages/{name}/`
2. Package name: `@superfunctions/{name}`
3. Add to workspace (already covered by `packages/*`)
4. Update dependent packages

### Creating Artifacts

1. Function-specific: `{function}/.conduct/{artifact}.md`
2. Shared/root: `_conduct/{artifact}.md`
3. Use consistent naming: `implementation.md`, `spec.md`, `audit_report.md`, etc.

### Working with Turbo

```bash
# Run task across all packages
turbo run build
turbo run test

# Run for specific package
turbo run build --filter=authfn

# Run with dependencies
turbo run build --filter=authfn...

# Clear cache
turbo run clean
```

## 📚 Important Files

### Root Configuration

- `package.json` - Workspace and script definitions
- `turbo.json` - Turbo build configuration
- `tsconfig.json` - TypeScript base config (if exists)

### Package Configuration

- `package.json` - Package metadata, dependencies, scripts
- `tsconfig.json` - TypeScript configuration
- `vitest.config.ts` - Test configuration
- `pyproject.toml` - Python package configuration

### Documentation

- `README.md` - Package overview and usage
- `SPEC.md` - Technical specification (common in larger functions)
- `.conduct/*.md` - Implementation plans, audits, tasks

## 🔍 Finding Code

### Search Patterns

- **Function implementations**: `{function}/typescript/src/` or `{function}/python/{function}/`
- **Tests**: `__tests__/`, `tests/`, `*.test.ts`, `test_*.py`
- **Types**: `types.ts`, `models.py`, `src/types/`
- **Adapters**: `packages/http-*/`, `packages/python-*/`, `adapters/`
- **Examples**: `examples/`, `{function}/examples/`

### Key Directories

```
superfunctions/
├── {function}/              # Core function packages
│   ├── typescript/          # TS implementation
│   ├── python/              # Python implementation
│   ├── .conduct/            # Artifacts
│   ├── README.md            # Documentation
│   └── SPEC.md              # Specification (if exists)
├── packages/                # Shared packages
│   ├── {name}/              # @superfunctions/{name}
│   └── python-{name}/       # Python shared packages
└── _conduct/                # Root artifacts
```

## 🚀 Best Practices

### Super functions ecosystem (Very important)

- Reuse shared packages from `packages/` folder like http abstraction, db abstraction, etc.
- Never duplicate shared code like http adapters, db abstractions, etc.
- Don't reexport http-adapters etc - end consumers of the core function package will use the adapters directly. Refer `authfn` implementation for usage of core http router, core db, http adapters and db interface usage.
- Function packages that accept a `@superfunctions/db` `Adapter` must wrap the incoming adapter internally with their own schema, for example `wrapWithSchema(config.database, getSchema(...))`, before passing it to services/storage. Do not require app consumers to pass `adapterSchema` to `drizzleAdapter`, `kyselyAdapter`, `prismaAdapter`, or `memoryAdapter`; `adapterSchema` is a deprecated compatibility escape hatch for direct app-level adapter use.

### Code Organization

- Keep shared code in `packages/`
- Keep function-specific code in `{function}/`
- Use TypeScript for type safety
- Provide Python SDKs for backend-focused functions
- Write comprehensive tests

### Documentation

- Update README.md with usage examples
- Create SPEC.md for complex functions
- Document breaking changes
- Keep artifacts in `.conduct/` folders

### Testing

- Use Vitest for TypeScript
- Use pytest for Python
- Maintain high test coverage
- Test adapters separately

### Versioning

- Follow semantic versioning
- Coordinate versions across language SDKs
- Document migration guides for breaking changes

## 🔗 Related Resources

- **Repository**: https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions
- **License**: MIT (most packages) / Apache-2.0 (some packages)
- **Organization**: 21n
- **Contact**: hello@21n.org

## 📝 Notes for AI Agents

1. **Always check both TypeScript and Python** implementations when working on core functions
2. **Respect the naming conventions** - shared packages use `@superfunctions/`, functions use simple names
3. **Create artifacts in `.conduct/` folders**, not in root or arbitrary locations
4. **Avoid nested monorepos** - use subfolders within the main Turbo monorepo
5. **Use Turbo commands** for cross-package operations
6. **Check existing patterns** in similar functions before implementing new features
7. **Maintain consistency** across TypeScript and Python SDKs
8. **Update workspaces** in root `package.json` when adding new packages
9. **Follow existing test patterns** (Vitest for TS, pytest for Python)
10. **Document thoroughly** - this is a developer-focused ecosystem

---

**Build Tool**: Turbo v2.0.0

# Python resource typing and CI readiness

Date: 2026-10-23. Baseline: `5b3467b8a3c6d754a7f408732106600cf4eb7fe6`.

## Reproduction and changes

A fresh normal Python 3.11 environment reproduced the hosted runner's 11 Ruff
errors. Import cleanup exposed 15 configured-mypy errors, including all resource
factories returning `object`, collection defaults annotated nonoptional but
initialized with `None`, the optional WebSockets import fallback, binary-frame
typing, and an unannotated stream return.

All nine resource classes now live at module scope, receive the same HTTP client
through their constructor, and are returned by their existing factories with
concrete types. This makes the advertised public methods visible to type checkers.
An AST comparison verified that all 25 existing resource method bodies are
unchanged except replacing the captured `client` with `self._client`; request
paths, payloads, parsing and public method signatures remain intact. A regression
exercises all nine resource groups and verifies separate clients retain their own
base URL.

Collection fields on aggregate bots, meeting metadata and API errors now use
independent default factories. Their existing post-init normalization of explicit
`None` from untyped callers remains; tests cover normalization and instance
isolation. The wheel includes `py.typed` for installed-package consumers.

The WebSocket connector and connection use small structural protocols instead of
an incompatible module/fallback assignment. Runtime module patching and the
missing-dependency error remain available. Frame parsing accepts the actual
`str | bytes` transport union. Invalid UTF-8 binary JSON is ignored alongside
invalid JSON, preserving the subsequent valid frames. The existing canonical
status/participant/error shape checks and ping-task cancellation are retained.
A real loopback server sends invalid UTF-8, invalid JSON, an invalid status shape,
a valid binary status frame and a valid text participant frame; only the two valid
frames are yielded before clean close.

Response envelopes and event payloads keep their existing dynamic dictionary/Any
contracts. This checkpoint does not claim comprehensive entity validation or
redesign those APIs. No type ignores, removed tests, weakened check flags, or
new/pinned production dependencies were introduced.

## Validation

| Environment | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Fresh Python 3.11.14 / WebSockets 17.3 / mypy 2.4.0 / pytest 9.1.1 | Actual `scripts/ci-run-python-package.mjs recfn/python` passes normal installation, wheel+sdist build, Ruff, configured full mypy over 19 source/test files, and 17 tests |
| Fresh installed wheel, Python 3.11.14 / WebSockets 17.3 | Strict public-resource consumer, consumer runtime, all 17 tests, and `pip check` pass |
| Fresh installed wheel, actual Python 3.9.6 / minimum WebSockets 12.0 | Strict public-resource consumer, consumer runtime, all 17 tests, and `pip check` pass |
| Actual Python 3.9.6 source/test checks | Full mypy with explicit `--python-version 3.9` passes all 19 files; Ruff passes |

The source retains its existing configured mypy settings; only the installed-wheel
consumer is checked with `--strict`. The explicit 3.9 check supplements the
configuration's 3.10 target and establishes minimum-version parsing/type evidence
with dependencies installed for that interpreter.

The original 14 tests remain, with three additional regressions. The TypeScript
`@recfn/core` producer was rebuilt before the cross-language frame-schema check.
For copied wheel tests, `RECFN_CONTRACT_ROOT` selects that checkout rather than
skipping the producer comparison. `PYTHONPATH` was unset and imports were read back
from `site-packages/recfn/__init__.py`. The current WebSockets test emits one
unsuppressed deprecation warning because its server fixture uses the legacy API
shared with WebSockets 12.0; the SDK continues to use the installed package's
normal top-level connector.

Minimum WebSockets was selected only in the disposable test environment with
`websockets==12.0`; the package requirement remains `websockets>=12.0`. Both wheel
installs used normal pip resolution. The inspected wheel includes `recfn/py.typed`
and has SHA-256
`244d6931b5e644015eccb7b2dea7dc490f2bdef1b66fb1cd846c4b8f55ed47b2`.
README instructions were added after that wheel build; validated Python source,
package contents and consumer fixtures are unchanged.

- `/tmp/rec-python311-fixed-ci-oct23.log`

malformed entity handling, or the other original RecFn readiness gates. No live

Date: 2026-10-23. Baseline: `65c612d56a72d2f62b9357d94e06cea443bbef6d`.

## Requirement and boundary

Original REC-004 prohibits raw recordings on plaintext disk (apart from an explicit
local-development opt-out) and requires encryption at rest through the storage
adapter. The streaming encoder previously persisted its encoded WAV/MP4 output as
a plaintext temporary file. This change encrypts that server capture scratch by
default, with no plaintext fallback or opt-out. It does not establish the separate
storage adapter encryption guarantee: passing `encryption: true` is not proof that
a configured adapter encrypts its backing store. Provider capture, deployment,
and external storage encryption attestation remain open.

## Implementation

FFmpeg stdout feeds an authenticated encrypted file through awaited bounded writes.
Each 64 KiB plaintext record uses AES-256-GCM, a fresh random 12-byte nonce, a
16-byte tag, and authenticated record index and length. The per-artifact 256-bit
key exists only in process memory. No key sidecar or recoverable key is written.
Files use exclusive creation and mode 0600 in the owned temporary directory.
The existing shared OAuth vault encrypts individual token values; it does not
provide a bounded media-file primitive, so this implementation uses Node crypto
without new dependencies or a duplicate storage adapter.

Authenticated bounded reads patch RIFF sizes in memory; every rewrite receives a
fresh nonce. Stream reads verify the whole record before yielding its plaintext.
Length changes, truncation, reordering, and authentication failure reject reads.
Full media inspection and decoder validation receive plaintext only through pipes.
Because ffprobe cannot infer WAV duration from a nonseekable stdin format header,
validation now derives duration from packet presentation times and durations,
while parsing bounded lines rather than buffering all packet metadata.

The default encoded-byte allowance remains 1 GiB. Ciphertext adds exactly 28 bytes
per 64 KiB record, including a final partial record: `N + ceil(N / 65536) * 28`.
For a full 1 GiB recording this is 458,752 additional bytes. Filesystem allocation
rounding and directory metadata are additional; this is not a global physical disk
quota. Node and Web stream queues explicitly count bytes, preserving backpressure.
Public artifact size/content type/stream contents remain ordinary encoded media.
Worker uploads continue using the existing streaming artifact interface.

Dispose destroys and joins active readers, closes the file, zeros owned key and
pending buffers, and removes the capture directory. Existing capture cancellation,
quota, encoder failure, and upload cleanup paths use this same disposal. A killed
worker leaves ciphertext, loses its process-only key, and closes its encoder pipes.
It does not automatically remove crash remnants or resume an incomplete recording.
Deployment cleanup/admission remains necessary. This protects files deliberately
written by the capture implementation; host swap, core dumps, privileged process
inspection, and adapter-owned files need their own deployment controls. It does
not promise secure erasure of every transient plaintext memory copy.

## Local validation

Node 20.20.0; FFmpeg and ffprobe 9.0.2. No live meeting or provider was contacted.

- Focused native suite: 30 tests across five files, including actual WAV/MP4/WebM
  output, exact PCM bytes, storage/upload deadlines, cipher integrity, boundary
  patches, active-reader disposal, and real killed-worker cleanup.
- Full server suite: 258 tests across 46 files.
- The killed-worker fixture starts an owned native encoder, waits for at least one
  ciphertext record on disk, sends actual SIGKILL to the worker, verifies encoder
  PID disappearance, checks that only ciphertext remains without a key sidecar,
  then removes its owned scratch. No guessed/unrelated PID is terminated.
- The first focused run failed with EBADF because the new file was opened
  write-only; changing exclusive creation from `wx` to `wx+` fixed authenticated
  reads. The subsequent focused and full suites passed without timeout changes.

The existing synthetic fixture generated 3600 seconds of 64x64 RGB24 at 30 fps,
16 kHz mono PCM, and 108000 video frames. With 128 MiB V8 old-space (reported total
heap limit 184,549,376 bytes), capture plus full validation took 37.401 seconds,
including 3.192 seconds after both producer EOFs; total storage/hash/frame-count
acceptance took 38.467 seconds. Sampled Node RSS was 134,103,040 bytes and encoder/
probe child RSS 38,895,616 bytes. Encoded size was 30,749,416 bytes and independently
probed duration 3600.064063 seconds. All 108000 frames decoded; upload/download
SHA-256 matched `22009a7ae5c2f615af4246c02a15bfa6fcc74a4bb7015bd169bbf947ad14523e`.
Only the fixture storage directory remained before its final recursive cleanup.
These low-complexity accelerated frames are not representative camera motion or
live provider-paced evidence. The local storage fixture deliberately stores the
uploaded plaintext media to independently probe it; it does not attest storage
adapter encryption.

```sh
npm test --workspace=@recfn/server
node --max-old-space-size=128 recfn/.conduct/media-streaming-acceptance.mjs
```

`/tmp/rec-encrypted-hour.json` (also retained beside this note).

payload.input:
text(await tools.exec_command({cmd:"cat > recfn/.conduct/recording-scratch-cleanup-readiness.md <<'EOF'
# Owned recording scratch cleanup

This extends encrypted capture scratch with bounded, ownership-aware reclamation.
It preserves the original recording/privacy/resource-lifecycle requirements; it
is not recovery of a crashed recording or a deployment-wide disk quota.

## Host configuration and lifecycle

`createRecordingScratch({ directory, cleanup? })` creates a new private root or
opens an existing root bearing its exact immutable marker. The parent must exist;
pass its canonical absolute path (for example, resolve macOS `/tmp` aliases with
`realpath`). An existing unmarked directory is deliberately not adopted. Root and
capture directories must be owned by the effective UID, with no group/other access.
Metadata files are exclusively created, synced, read-only, bounded to 4096 bytes,
and opened without following symlinks; hard-linked metadata/media is rejected.
The root marker pins its canonical path and random identity. Each manager also
pins root device/inode and rechecks them before managed mutation.

The factory performs one bounded cleanup sweep. Retain the manager and pass it to
`createBotWorker({ captureOptions: { scratch }, environment: 'production', ... })`.
Production workers require managed scratch with supported host identity; the check
also runs at capture startup. Development keeps the existing unmanaged
`temporaryDirectory` compatibility path, and direct capture can use managed scratch
without cleanup support. Neither path is labeled production-safe automatically.
The HTTP-only `createRecFnServer` does not create workers or own capture scratch.

```ts
const scratch = await createRecordingScratch({
  directory: '/var/lib/recfn/recording-scratch', // canonical, dedicated, host-local
  cleanup: { maxEntries: 128, maxBytes: 8 * 1024 ** 3, maxDurationMs: 1000 },
});
const worker = createBotWorker({ ...workerConfig, environment: 'production',
  captureOptions: { scratch } });
// Report scratch.lastCleanup; retry incomplete scans using the same manager.
const report = await scratch.cleanup();
// On shutdown, stop dequeuing first, then:
await worker.cancelCaptures();
await scratch.close();
```

results. A manager keeps an unfinished directory scan open across calls, so a

# RecFn

Self-hosted meeting recording SDK for the Superfunctions ecosystem. Record meetings from Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams; transcribe with ASR providers; search transcripts; and deliver events via webhooks.

## Packages

- **`recfn`** (core) — Types, interfaces, and utilities
- **`recfn-server`** — HTTP API server
- **`recfn/client`** — TypeScript HTTP client
- **`recfn/desktop`** — Desktop capture and recorder
- **`recfn/python`** — Python SDK
- **`recfn/platforms/*`** — Platform adapters (Zoom, Meet, Teams)
- **`recfn/adapters/*`** — ASR adapters (Deepgram, AssemblyAI, Google STT)

```ts
import { createRecFnServer, createMemoryStore, MemoryStorageAdapter } from '@recfn/server';

const store = createMemoryStore();
const storage = new MemoryStorageAdapter();

  store,
  storage,
  validateApiKey: (key) => ({ namespace: 'default', apiKey: key }),
});
```

`store.deleteBot()` remains the database-only transaction primitive; use the
coordinator or HTTP endpoint for external cleanup. The database adapter must
support transactions and serialize writes to the bot root. File-backed SQLite,
real local files, and the SearchFn memory index have failure/reopen and concurrent
producer coverage. Other database isolation modes and remote storage/search
providers require their own acceptance; this is not live-provider evidence.

### Bot media finalization

Bot workers require `ffmpeg` (PCM/AAC and libx264 encoders) and `ffprobe` on
`PATH`. Audio/video are encoded concurrently through bounded pipes into a
quota-limited temporary artifact; raw media is not spooled. Validated artifacts
stream to shared storage and are disposed on success/failure. The worker uses
`captureToFile`; `captureFromStream` remains a bounded buffer convenience API.

`BotWorkerConfig.captureOptions` selects executable paths, a private temporary
parent directory, and limits. File capture defaults to a 1 GiB encoded-output
quota, 64 MiB maximum individual input chunk, and four-hour capture deadline.
There is no default cumulative raw-byte quota; callers can set `maxInputBytes`.
The buffer API defaults to 64 MiB output and caps configuration at 256 MiB. File
output may be configured below 4 GiB. Quota/deadline failures reject the recording
instead of publishing truncated media. Encoder draining after input EOF, probing,
and full decoder validation each have a 60-second deadline. Stop dequeuing jobs,
then call `worker.cancelCaptures()` to abort active capture and release artifacts.

Zoom queues copy SDK buffers and cap each stream at 32 MiB. Browser capture caps
queued blob bytes and its Node stream queue at 8 MiB each. A coordinated bounded
audio split applies backpressure to both recording and real-time ASR consumers.
Overflow is an explicit capture failure, not frame dropping. Provider internals
and custom producers retain their own backpressure obligations. Low-complexity
one-hour generated-media acceptance is documented in
[streaming readiness](.conduct/media-streaming-readiness.md); live provider and
representative workload acceptance remain unfinished.

Adapters must declare `AudioChunk.encoding`: interleaved signed 16-bit
little-endian PCM (`pcm_s16le`), or consecutive bytes from one WebM/Ogg audio
container. PCM sample rate and channel count must remain constant and frames
must contain complete samples. For encoded audio, decoder metadata determines
the resulting sample format. Audio-only recordings are finalized as WAV.

text(await tools.exec_command({cmd:"cat > recfn/.conduct/bot-admission-readiness.md <<'EOF'
# Atomic namespace bot-row admission

Original LIMIT-001 and SPEC “Limits/caps” require configurable concurrent bots per
namespace, default 100. SPEC also assigns recording file-size limits to storage;
it does not specify a global operating-system scratch quota. This checkpoint
addresses admission of persisted nonterminal bot rows. It does not establish an
exact count of live provider connections/capture processes: cross-worker join
ownership and durable queue handoff remain separate required lifecycle work.

## Reproduction

On the preceding built source, a cap of one admitted two concurrent check/create
operations. One older active bot hidden behind two newer terminal rows passed the
same check. `listBots` capped results to 100 and the middleware filtered only that
page, excluding `finalizing` as well. Calendar scheduling bypassed the check:
with `RECFN_MAX_CONCURRENT_BOTS=1`, one local poll created two bots. No external
calendar or meeting provider was called for these reproductions.

## Shared transaction authority

The built-in store now performs create and status mutation through a namespace
transaction. Its **first database operation** upserts a guard row with a fresh
nonce, acquiring the namespace write lock before any count snapshot. It then counts
all namespace bots whose status is neither `done` nor `error`, and inserts only
when capacity exists. The indexed database count is independent of API pagination.
Finalizing, leaving, and left bots remain counted. The REST route, calendar
scheduler and direct built-in store creation therefore share one authority.

Status mutations acquire namespace authority before the bot aggregate's deletion
fence. Terminal-to-nonterminal direct updates require capacity; terminalization
and ongoing active transitions permit draining. A failed insert or mutation rolls
back with its transaction. Deletion retains the namespace policy row even after
all bots are gone. The existing deletion/producer fence remains in effect.

`createDbStore({ adapter, maxConcurrentBots })` and
`createMemoryStore({ maxConcurrentBots })` accept a positive safe integer, defaulting
to `RECFN_MAX_CONCURRENT_BOTS` or 100. Each namespace persists the maximum on its
policy row; processes configured differently fail closed. Quota rejection uses
HTTP 429 / `RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED`. The API no longer makes a separate racy precheck.
Production stores must advertise the atomic namespace-admission capability in
addition to durability. Custom callback stores do not gain that capability merely
by providing `createBot` or `listBots`.

Supported built-in integration identities are shared memory, Kysely and Drizzle,
with transaction and upsert capabilities enabled. Source inspection establishes:

- Shared memory already serializes all captured adapter operations and internal
  CRUD through its own queue, including snapshot/rollback transactions. RecFn
  reuses this implementation and adds no per-store mutex.
- Kysely emits native `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` for PostgreSQL/SQLite and
  `INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` for MySQL before a read.
- Drizzle emits the corresponding native write for PostgreSQL/MySQL. Its SQLite
  adapter explicitly does not support async transactions and is rejected.

The nonce forces an actual guard-row update. The transaction must hold that write
lock until commit and must not perform an earlier application read snapshot.
Serialization/deadlock/busy failures propagate rather than bypassing admission;
there is no unsafe automatic fallback. Native acceptance here is Kysely with
file-backed SQLite only. Other SQL dialect/provider configurations still require
native acceptance. Integration IDs are trusted host metadata, not authentication
against a caller that deliberately spoofs an entire adapter implementation.

Prisma and unknown adapters fail closed for bot creation/status admission. Their
generic upsert capability does not prove a native first-write operation; some
Prisma/backend combinations may read before updating. Required Prisma/backend
compatibility remains open rather than being inferred from a host opt-in flag.

## Required migration and configuration changes

Stop API producers, calendar schedulers, and workers before migration. Apply the
new `botAdmission` model from `getRecFnSchema()` with primary/unique `id`, unique
`namespace`, numeric `maximum`, and string `nonce`. Existing bot rows and indexes
remain unchanged. Seed each existing namespace with its explicitly chosen policy:
`id` is lowercase SHA-256 of UTF-8 namespace, `maximum` is the configured positive
integer, and `nonce` is a fresh UUID. New namespaces initialize their policy within
the admission transaction. Seeding existing namespaces makes the policy explicit
before any first-operation failure/rollback.

To change a persisted policy, stop all writers, update that namespace's `maximum`
and nonce transactionally, change every producer/worker configuration to match,
and restart. A lower cap can be below current occupancy: new admission and
reactivation reject while terminal transitions drain existing bots. Do not clear
policy rows to bypass a mismatch. The store never silently raises a persisted
limit. Deployment operators retain responsibility for applying schema migration
and validating their actual SQL adapter/isolation configuration.

## Queue and process ownership boundary

Bot creation commits before queue enqueue. A queue may accept a job and then lose
its acknowledgement; its interface cannot prove that an exception means no send.
The bot therefore remains `creating` and continues consuming capacity on enqueue
failure. Retrying a fresh creation at capacity returns 429. No uncertain queued
operation is erased or released automatically. Inspect namespace bot state and
queue/worker evidence; retry the existing bot's job or mark terminal only after
establishing that its original worker/provider operation has stopped. There is no
new idempotency/outbox guarantee in this checkpoint.

The worker's current read/check of `creating` is not an atomic cross-worker claim.
Multiple workers could still race to join the same bot, and database-only direct
aggregate deletion does not prove external provider cleanup. Thus row admission
must not be described as exact running-capture admission. Durable outbox/idempotent
join ownership is the next required slice. Existing ambiguous storage producer
intents, scratch byte limits/cleanup, and adapter encryption-attestation gaps are
preserved. Aggregate physical disk quota is still a deployment concern.

## Validation

Pending final receipts. No live provider or deployment is used.
EOF
python3 - <<'PY'
p='recfn/README.md';s=open(p).read();needle='### Bot worker\n';insert='''### Bot admission policy

Built-in stores enforce a persisted per-namespace nonterminal bot limit, default
100 (`RECFN_MAX_CONCURRENT_BOTS`), configurable with
`createDbStore({ adapter, maxConcurrentBots: 100, durable: true })` or
`createMemoryStore({ maxConcurrentBots: 100 })`. API creation, calendar scheduling,
and direct store creation share the transaction; finalizing bots remain counted,
and direct reactivation requires available capacity. Full capacity returns 429.

Existing installations must migrate the `botAdmission` model and seed namespace
policies before restarting writers. Policy changes require stopped writers and a
matching database/configuration update; lowering below occupancy permits draining.
Supported paths are shared memory and transactional native-upsert Kysely/Drizzle;
Prisma, unknown adapters, and Drizzle SQLite remain unsupported for this admission
contract. Native acceptance covers Kysely SQLite, not every database deployment.
See [admission and migration details](.conduct/bot-admission-readiness.md).

An ambiguous queue-enqueue failure retains its creating bot and capacity. It does
not prove that no worker will run. Reconcile the existing operation before retrying
or releasing it. Atomic cross-worker join ownership/durable queue handoff remain
unfinished; this cap counts bot rows and does not prove an exact live-process cap.

''';s=s.replace(needle,insert+needle);open(p,'w').write(s)
PY","workdir":"/Volumes/Dev/n/worktrees/superfunctions/recfn-sf-next-readiness","max_output_tokens":300}));

before any first-operation failure/rollback.

To change a persisted policy, stop all writers, update that namespace's `maximum`
and nonce transactionally, change every producer/worker configuration to match,
and restart. A lower cap can be below current occupancy: new admission and
reactivation reject while terminal transitions drain existing bots. Do not clear
policy rows to bypass a mismatch. The store never silently raises a persisted
limit. Deployment operators retain responsibility for applying schema migration
and validating their actual SQL adapter/isolation configuration.

## Queue and process ownership boundary

Bot creation commits before queue enqueue. A queue may accept a job and then lose
its acknowledgement; its interface cannot prove that an exception means no send.
The bot therefore remains `creating` and continues consuming capacity on enqueue
failure. Retrying a fresh creation at capacity returns 429. No uncertain queued
operation is erased or released automatically. Inspect namespace bot state and
queue/worker evidence; retry the existing bot's job or mark terminal only after
establishing that its original worker/provider operation has stopped. There is no
new idempotency/outbox guarantee in this checkpoint.

The worker's current read/check of `creating` is not an atomic cross-worker claim.
Multiple workers could still race to join the same bot, and database-only direct
aggregate deletion does not prove external provider cleanup. Thus row admission
must not be described as exact running-capture admission. Durable outbox/idempotent
join ownership is the next required slice. Existing ambiguous storage producer
intents, scratch byte limits/cleanup, and adapter encryption-attestation gaps are
preserved. Aggregate physical disk quota is still a deployment concern.

## Validation

Pending final receipts. No live provider or deployment is used.
